name: Energy-based neural PDE solvers (Deep Ritz)
summary: Networks can minimize the variational energy of a mechanics problem instead of a residual, turning the principle of minimum potential energy into the training objective.
sources: Samaniego et al. (2020). "An energy approach to the solution of partial differential equations in computational mechanics via machine learning: Concepts, implementation and applications". *Comput. Methods Appl. Mech. Eng.* 362, 112790. [arXiv:1908.10407](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.10407)

name: Physics-informed networks for Navier–Stokes
summary: PINNs penalize the Navier–Stokes residual in the loss to reconstruct velocity and pressure from sparse data; flow problems are the main testbed for scientific-ML surrogates.
sources: Cai et al. (2021). "Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for fluid mechanics: a review". *Acta Mech. Sin.* 37, 1727. [arXiv:2105.09506](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.09506)

Raissi, Perdikaris & Karniadakis (2019). "Physics-informed neural networks: A deep learning framework for solving forward and inverse problems involving nonlinear partial differential equations". *J. Comput. Phys.* 378, 686. [doi:10.1016/j.jcp.2018.10.045](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcp.2018.10.045)

name: Molecular dynamics integrates Hamilton's equations
summary: MD is numerical Hamiltonian mechanics for N particles; Nosé's extended Hamiltonian adds a thermostat variable so that the deterministic flow samples the canonical ensemble.
sources: Verlet (1967). "Computer 'Experiments' on Classical Fluids. I. Thermodynamical Properties of Lennard-Jones Molecules". *Phys. Rev.* 159, 98. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.159.98](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.159.98)
Nosé (1984). "A unified formulation of the constant temperature molecular dynamics methods". *J. Chem. Phys.* 81, 511. [doi:10.1063/1.447334](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.447334)

name: Lyapunov instability underlies MD ergodicity
summary: Many-particle MD trajectories are chaotic with positive Lyapunov exponents, so individual trajectories are irreproducible after picoseconds while time averages converge to ensemble averages; chaos is what makes MD statistics robust.

name: Hamiltonian (hybrid) Monte Carlo
summary: HMC proposes moves by integrating fictitious Hamiltonian dynamics with leapfrog; time reversibility and Liouville volume preservation make the Metropolis correction exact.

name: Symplectic integrators ↔ Hamiltonian flow
summary: Leapfrog/Verlet and other symplectic schemes are exact flows of a nearby 'shadow' Hamiltonian, so they preserve phase-space volume and show no secular energy drift; the integrator inherits the symplectic structure of Hamilton's equations.
breaks: Backward-error bound holds only for fixed step size; adaptive steps or dissipation destroy the shadow Hamiltonian.
sources: Verlet (1967). "Computer 'Experiments' on Classical Fluids. I. Thermodynamical Properties of Lennard-Jones Molecules". *Phys. Rev.* 159, 98. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.159.98](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.159.98)

name: Variational integrators and Ritz–Galerkin
summary: Discretizing the action rather than the equations gives variational integrators that are automatically symplectic and momentum-conserving (discrete Noether); finite elements are Ritz minimization of an energy functional.

name: Finite elements born in structural elasticity
summary: The finite element method grew out of structural and elasticity analysis (Courant's 1943 variational triangles, 1950s aircraft stress analysis) and is a Ritz–Galerkin minimization of the elastic energy.

name: DNS and spectral solvers ↔ turbulence
summary: Direct numerical simulation must resolve from the integral scale L down to the Kolmogorov scale η, so grid points grow as Re^{9/4}; pseudospectral FFT methods and LES closures are the workhorses of turbulence research.

name: N-body integrators ↔ celestial mechanics
summary: Long-term Solar System integrations use symplectic map methods (Wisdom–Holman splitting into Kepler drift plus interaction kick) and regularization for close encounters.
map: H=H_{\rm Kep}+H_{\rm int},\ \ e^{hL_H}\approx e^{\frac h2L_{\rm int}}e^{hL_{\rm Kep}}e^{\frac h2L_{\rm int}}

name: Lyapunov spectra and shadowing in numerics
summary: Lyapunov exponents are computed by tangent-map integration with repeated QR (Gram–Schmidt) reorthonormalization; the shadowing lemma justifies trusting chaotic numerical orbits statistically even though each diverges from the true one.

name: Standard map = leapfrog kicked rotor
summary: Chirikov's standard map is the symplectic-Euler discretization of a pendulum and the exact flow of the kicked rotor; KAM theory explains why symplectic integrators keep invariant tori and stay stable for exponentially long times.
breaks: Correspondence with the continuous pendulum holds only for small step K; for K≳1 the map's global chaos is a discretization artifact.

name: Rutherford scattering discovered the nucleus
summary: Rutherford's classical Coulomb-orbit cross-section, fitted to Geiger–Marsden α data, revealed the atomic nucleus; the same formula happens to be exact in quantum mechanics.
sources: Rutherford (1911). "The scattering of α and β particles by matter and the structure of the atom". *Phil. Mag.* 21, 669. [doi:10.1080/14786440508637080](https://doi.org/10.1080/14786440508637080)

name: Liouville, recurrence and the arrow of time
summary: Time-reversal-invariant Hamiltonian flow preserves phase-space volume, so fine-grained Gibbs entropy is constant and Poincaré recurrence holds; irreversibility needs coarse-graining plus a low-entropy past.

name: Force Concept Inventory ↔ Newton's laws
summary: Newton's three laws are the content probed by the Force Concept Inventory; PER shows students hold impetus-like preconceptions, and interactive engagement roughly doubles the normalized gain.
sources: Hestenes, Wells & Swackhamer (1992). "Force concept inventory". *Phys. Teach.* 30, 141. [doi:10.1119/1.2343497](https://doi.org/10.1119/1.2343497)

Hake (1998). "Interactive-engagement versus traditional methods: A six-thousand-student survey of mechanics test data for introductory physics courses". *Am. J. Phys.* 66, 64. [doi:10.1119/1.18809](https://doi.org/10.1119/1.18809)

name: Conformal maps for 2D potential flow and lift
summary: Planar irrotational incompressible flow is an analytic complex potential; Joukowski conformal maps generate airfoils and the Blasius contour integral gives the Kutta–Joukowski lift.

name: Small divisors and analytic estimates in KAM
summary: Lindstedt perturbation series diverge because of small denominators k·ω; KAM proves torus survival for Diophantine frequencies by Newton iteration with Cauchy estimates on shrinking complex analyticity strips.

name: Inverse scattering via analytic scattering data
summary: The inverse scattering transform solves KdV and NLS by mapping initial data to scattering data analytic in the spectral parameter, reconstructed through a Riemann–Hilbert (Gelfand–Levitan) problem; solitons are bound-state poles.

name: Damped oscillator response ↔ causality and Kramers–Kronig
summary: The driven damped oscillator's susceptibility has poles only in the lower half ω-plane because the response is causal, so its real and imaginary parts obey Kramers–Kronig; its impulse response is the retarded Green's function.

name: Hamilton–Jacobi PDE ↔ method of characteristics
summary: The Hamilton–Jacobi equation is a first-order nonlinear PDE whose characteristics are exactly Hamilton's equations; complete integrals give generating functions of canonical transformations.

name: Stokeslet = Green's function of Stokes flow
summary: The Oseen tensor (Stokeslet) is the Green's function of the Stokes equations; boundary-integral, slender-body and hydrodynamic-interaction methods superpose it.

name: Acoustic waves ↔ retarded Green's function
summary: Sound radiated by sources is the source convolved with the retarded Green's function of the wave equation; Huygens' sharp-front principle holds in odd spatial dimensions.

name: Floquet theory of the Mathieu equation
summary: Parametric resonance is governed by Floquet–Hill theory of linear ODEs with periodic coefficients; Mathieu characteristic exponents define the instability tongues near ω = 2ω₀/n.

name: Poisson brackets ↔ commutators; Koopman–von Neumann
summary: Dirac's rule {f,g} → [f̂,ĝ]/iħ maps Hamiltonian mechanics onto Hilbert-space operators; conversely Koopman–von Neumann write classical mechanics as unitary evolution on L²(phase space).
breaks: Groenewold–van Hove: no quantization map preserves all brackets beyond quadratic polynomials.

name: Normal modes = generalized eigenproblem
summary: Small oscillations about equilibrium reduce to the symmetric generalized eigenproblem Kv = ω²Mv; normal modes are the orthogonal eigenvectors guaranteed by the spectral theorem.

name: Principal axes = spectral theorem for the inertia tensor
summary: The inertia tensor is real symmetric, so it has orthogonal eigenvectors (principal axes) and real eigenvalues (principal moments); rotational kinetic energy is diagonal in that basis.

name: Phase space as a symplectic manifold
summary: Phase space is the cotangent bundle T*Q with symplectic 2-form ω = dp∧dq; Hamilton's equations are ι_X ω = dH, Poisson brackets come from ω^{-1}, and Liouville's theorem is conservation of the volume form ω^n.

name: Strain compatibility = flat metric; defects = torsion and curvature
summary: Saint-Venant compatibility is the vanishing Riemann tensor of the deformed metric g = δ + 2ε; in the geometric theory of defects dislocations are torsion and disclinations curvature of a material connection.

name: Fictitious forces as connection coefficients
summary: Coriolis and centrifugal forces are the Christoffel symbols of rotating coordinates in flat space; writing Newton's law covariantly prefigures the equivalence principle.

name: Resonant sensors: Q, bandwidth and thermal force noise
summary: Mechanical and electrical resonators used as sensors are driven damped oscillators; Q sets the bandwidth f₀/Q and the lock-in readout, and via fluctuation–dissipation the thermal force-noise floor.

name: Least squares born from orbit determination
summary: Gauss developed least squares and the normal error law to recover the orbit of Ceres (1801–1809); χ² fitting of orbital elements remains the template for parameter estimation.

name: Kepler's hidden SO(4) and the Runge–Lenz vector
summary: The conserved Laplace–Runge–Lenz vector together with L generates SO(4) for bound Kepler orbits, explaining closed ellipses (Bertrand) and, once quantized, the n² degeneracy of hydrogen (Pauli 1926).

name: KdV hierarchies ↔ infinite-dimensional Lie algebras
summary: Integrable soliton equations come in hierarchies attached to Kac–Moody algebras (Drinfeld–Sokolov); the Lax pair is a flat connection in a loop algebra and tau functions carry representations of infinite-dimensional groups.
sources: Drinfeld & Sokolov (1984). "Lie algebras and equations of Korteweg-de Vries type". *J. Sov. Math.* 30, 1975. [doi:10.1007/bf02105860](https://doi.org/10.1007/bf02105860)
Jimbo & Miwa (1983). "Solitons and Infinite Dimensional Lie Algebras". *Publ. RIMS Kyoto* 19, 943. [doi:10.2977/prims/1195182017](https://doi.org/10.2977/prims/1195182017)

name: Rotation group SO(3) ↔ rigid-body motion
summary: A rigid body's configuration space is SO(3); Euler's equations are the Lie–Poisson equations on so(3)*, and the inertia tensor defines a left-invariant metric whose geodesics are torque-free motions.

name: Invariance of the action → Noether currents
summary: Noether's theorem is a statement about the variational principle: a continuous transformation leaving the action invariant up to a boundary term yields a conserved quantity; cyclic coordinates are the simplest case.
map: \delta L=\frac{dK}{dt}\Rightarrow Q=\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q}\delta q-K,\ \dot Q=0
sources: Noether (1918; English translation 1971). "Invariant variation problems". *Transport Theory Stat. Phys.* 1, 186. [doi:10.1080/00411457108231446](https://doi.org/10.1080/00411457108231446)

name: Kelvin circulation from particle-relabelling symmetry
summary: In the Lagrangian (Euler–Poincaré) formulation of ideal fluids, invariance under relabelling of fluid particles is a Noether symmetry whose charge is circulation; Kelvin's theorem and potential-vorticity conservation follow.
breaks: Exact only for ideal barotropic fluids; viscosity and baroclinic torques break it.

name: Newtonian mechanics as symmetry consequences
summary: The Galilean symmetry group of Newtonian mechanics (translations, rotations, boosts) fixes its conserved quantities; the Galilean boost charge gives uniform centre-of-mass motion.
sources: Noether (1918; English translation 1971). "Invariant variation problems". *Transport Theory Stat. Phys.* 1, 186. [doi:10.1080/00411457108231446](https://doi.org/10.1080/00411457108231446)

name: Noether's theorem ↔ energy, momentum, angular momentum
summary: The conservation laws of Newtonian mechanics are the Noether charges of time translation, space translation and rotation invariance of the action.
map: \partial L/\partial t=0\Rightarrow E=\dot q\,\partial L/\partial\dot q-L\ \text{conserved}
sources: Noether (1918; English translation 1971). "Invariant variation problems". *Transport Theory Stat. Phys.* 1, 186. [doi:10.1080/00411457108231446](https://doi.org/10.1080/00411457108231446)

name: Integrability = enough conserved charges in involution
summary: Liouville–Arnold integrability needs n Poisson-commuting conserved quantities; KdV has infinitely many, generated by commuting symmetry flows, which is why solitons survive collisions.

name: Elasticity as the Goldstone theory of broken translations
summary: A crystal breaks continuous translations; continuum elasticity is the effective theory of the corresponding Goldstone fields (displacements), and its sound waves are the Goldstone modes.
breaks: Broken rotations give no independent Goldstone modes (inverse Higgs); amorphous solids are elastic without long-range order.

name: Pitchfork bifurcation = Landau symmetry breaking
summary: The normal form of a Z2-symmetric pitchfork is gradient flow on a φ⁴ potential; the supercritical branch is mean-field spontaneous symmetry breaking with exponent 1/2.
breaks: No fluctuations or thermodynamic limit, so only mean-field exponents; Hopf bifurcations break time translation rather than an internal symmetry.

name: Kuramoto sync and Turing patterns as symmetry breaking
summary: Kuramoto synchronization is a U(1)-breaking transition with order parameter re^{iψ} and mean-field exponent 1/2; Turing patterns spontaneously break translation symmetry.
breaks: Driven-dissipative attractors with no free energy or detailed balance; the phase mode diffuses rather than propagating, and noise can restore the symmetry.

name: Galileo's square–cube law
summary: Galileo's 1638 argument that beam strength scales as L² while weight scales as L³ is the first scaling law and limits the size of animals and structures; Euler buckling follows the same logic.

name: Buckingham π ↔ Reynolds similarity
summary: Dimensional analysis reduces drag and flow problems to functions of a few dimensionless groups (Re, Ma, Fr), which is the basis of wind-tunnel scaling and dynamic similarity.
sources: Buckingham (1914). "On Physically Similar Systems; Illustrations of the Use of Dimensional Equations". *Phys. Rev.* 4, 345. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.4.345](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.4.345)

name: Re ≪ 1 regime and the scallop theorem
summary: At Re ≪ 1 inertia drops out and Stokes flow is linear and instantaneous, so reciprocal strokes give no net swimming (Purcell's scallop theorem); scaling arguments set what microswimmers can do.
sources: Purcell (1977). "Life at low Reynolds number". *Am. J. Phys.* 45, 3. [doi:10.1119/1.10903](https://doi.org/10.1119/1.10903)

name: Kolmogorov 1941 from dimensional analysis
summary: If the inertial range depends only on the dissipation rate ε and wavenumber k, dimensional analysis fixes the −5/3 spectrum and the Kolmogorov scale; intermittency corrections are the anomalous part beyond dimensional reasoning.

name: Newton to Lagrange via d'Alembert's principle
summary: For workless (ideal) constraints and potential forces, d'Alembert's principle of virtual work turns Newton's second law into the Euler–Lagrange equations in generalized coordinates and eliminates the constraint forces. Hamilton's principle restates the same dynamics as a variational principle.
map: \sum_i(\mathbf F_i-m_i\ddot{\mathbf r}_i)\cdot\delta\mathbf r_i=0\Rightarrow\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q_k}=\frac{\partial L}{\partial q_k}
breaks: Friction and nonholonomic constraints need Rayleigh dissipation functions or Lagrange multipliers; nonholonomic systems do not follow from a naive variational principle.

name: Liouville–Arnold integrability and its generic failure
summary: An n-degree-of-freedom Hamiltonian with n independent integrals in involution moves quasi-periodically on invariant tori and has action–angle variables. Poincaré showed that generic systems lack such integrals, and the mixed regular–chaotic phase space that remains is the conservative half of nonlinear dynamics.
sources: Hénon & Heiles (1964). "The applicability of the third integral of motion: Some numerical experiments". *Astron. J.* 69, 73. [doi:10.1086/109234](https://doi.org/10.1086/109234)

name: Rigid bodies as Lagrangian systems on SO(3)
summary: A body's orientation is a point of SO(3). With Euler angles as generalized coordinates, the heavy symmetric top's Lagrangian has cyclic φ and ψ, whose conjugate momenta L_z and L_3 (plus energy) make the top integrable and reduce it to one-dimensional motion in θ in an effective potential.

name: Small divisors in canonical perturbation theory
summary: Canonical perturbation theory removes a perturbation with a generating function whose Fourier coefficients carry small divisors k·ω, which blow up at resonances. KAM replaces the divergent series with a superconvergent Newton iteration of canonical transformations. It converges for Diophantine frequencies and nondegenerate H_0, so most tori persist.
map: H=H_0(\mathbf J)+\epsilon H_1(\mathbf J,\boldsymbol\theta),\quad S_{1,\mathbf k}=\frac{iH_{1,\mathbf k}(\mathbf J)}{\mathbf k\cdot\boldsymbol\omega(\mathbf J)}

name: Adiabatic invariant E/ω of a slowly varied oscillator
summary: In action–angle variables the oscillator's action is J=E/ω. When the frequency changes slowly compared with the period, J is an adiabatic invariant, with exponentially small changes for smooth variation. This was Einstein's 1911 Solvay answer to Lorentz's slowly shortened pendulum, and it is the classical root of Bohr–Sommerfeld quantization.

name: Point vortices: x and y as conjugate variables
summary: Kirchhoff showed that N point vortices in 2D ideal flow obey Hamilton's equations, with Γ_i x_i conjugate to y_i and a logarithmic interaction Hamiltonian. Configuration space is phase space, so a bounded domain has finite phase volume. Onsager used this to find negative-temperature states in which like-signed vortices cluster, a precursor of the 2D inverse cascade.
map: \Gamma_i\dot x_i=\frac{\partial H}{\partial y_i},\ \Gamma_i\dot y_i=-\frac{\partial H}{\partial x_i},\ H=-\frac{1}{4\pi}\sum_{i<j}\Gamma_i\Gamma_j\ln r_{ij}^2

name: Kepler's hidden SO(4) symmetry
summary: The Laplace–Runge–Lenz vector is conserved for the 1/r potential. Together with L, its Poisson brackets close on so(4) for bound orbits, which makes Kepler motion superintegrable. This explains why bound orbits close and why the energy depends on only one combination of the actions.

name: Liouville's theorem: conservative vs dissipative chaos
summary: Hamiltonian flow preserves phase-space volume (Liouville), so Lyapunov exponents come in ± pairs and attractors cannot exist; chaos instead fills chaotic seas on the energy shell. Dissipative flows contract volume onto strange attractors, e.g. the Lorenz flow, which contracts at the constant rate σ+1+β.
sources: Hénon & Heiles (1964). "The applicability of the third integral of motion: Some numerical experiments". *Astron. J.* 69, 73. [doi:10.1086/109234](https://doi.org/10.1086/109234)

name: KdV as a Liouville-integrable Hamiltonian field theory
summary: KdV is a Hamiltonian field equation with the Gardner bracket ∂_x(δ/δu). Its infinitely many conserved quantities from inverse scattering Poisson-commute, and the scattering data serve as action–angle variables (Zakharov–Faddeev). This extends Liouville integrability to infinitely many degrees of freedom.
sources: Gardner, Greene, Kruskal & Miura (1967). "Method for Solving the Korteweg-deVries Equation". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 19, 1095. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.19.1095](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.19.1095)

name: Euler's equations as a Lie–Poisson system on so(3)*
summary: Reducing T*SO(3) by rotation symmetry gives the Lie–Poisson bracket {L_i,L_j}=−ε_ijk L_k on the body angular momenta, in which Euler's equations are Hamiltonian. |L|² is a Casimir, so trajectories are intersections of the momentum sphere with the energy ellipsoid. The stable and unstable axes follow from the energy–Casimir method.
map: \{F,G\}=-\mathbf L\cdot(\nabla F\times\nabla G),\ \dot{\mathbf L}=\mathbf L\times\mathsf I^{-1}\mathbf L,\ C=|\mathbf L|^2

name: Cyclic coordinates and Noether's conserved momenta
summary: In Lagrangian mechanics the Newtonian conservation laws of momentum, angular momentum and energy follow from invariance under translations, rotations and time translations. A coordinate absent from L has a conserved conjugate momentum, and an L with no explicit time dependence conserves the energy function h.
map: \frac{\partial L}{\partial q_k}=0\Rightarrow p_k=\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q_k}=\text{const};\ \frac{\partial L}{\partial t}=0\Rightarrow h=\dot q_kp_k-L=\text{const}

name: Kelvin's circulation theorem from relabelling symmetry
summary: Ideal barotropic flow follows from Hamilton's principle written in fluid-particle labels. The action is invariant under mass-preserving relabelling of parcels, and Noether's theorem for this infinite-dimensional symmetry gives Kelvin's circulation theorem and the conservation of potential vorticity.
breaks: Viscosity and non-conservative forcing destroy the variational structure and with it the theorem.

name: Elastic P, S and Rayleigh waves
summary: Navier's equations of linear elasticity admit compressional (P) and shear (S) waves, with speeds set by the Lamé moduli, plus Rayleigh surface waves at ≈0.92 c_S for Poisson ratio 0.25. Acoustics in solids is linear elastodynamics, the basis of seismology and ultrasonic testing.

name: Kirchhoff's kinetic analogy: elastic rod and spinning top
summary: Kirchhoff showed that the equilibrium equations of a thin inextensible elastic rod are those of a heavy top, with arclength in place of time. Curvature–twist maps to angular velocity, bending and twisting stiffnesses map to moments of inertia, and end tension maps to gravity. The planar elastica is the pendulum equation, and helical rods are steady precessions.
map: s\leftrightarrow t,\ \boldsymbol\kappa(s)\leftrightarrow\boldsymbol\omega(t),\ (B,B,C)\leftrightarrow(I_1,I_1,I_3),\ \mathbf F\leftrightarrow Mg\hat{\mathbf z};\ EI\theta''+P\sin\theta=0
breaks: Rod shapes solve boundary-value problems in arclength (clamped or loaded ends), while tops solve initial-value problems in time. The analogy holds only for the statics of inextensible, unshearable rods and fails with self-contact, extensibility or shear.

name: KdV solitons from shallow-water Euler flow
summary: Scott Russell's 1834 solitary wave in a canal is an exact solution of the Korteweg–de Vries equation. KdV is derived from the ideal Euler equations for long, small-amplitude waves in shallow water, where weak nonlinearity balances weak dispersion. Deep-water waves instead give the nonlinear Schrödinger equation, envelope solitons and rogue-wave models.
sources: Gardner, Greene, Kruskal & Miura (1967). "Method for Solving the Korteweg-deVries Equation". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 19, 1095. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.19.1095](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.19.1095)

name: Sound as linearized compressible Euler flow
summary: Linearizing the compressible Euler and continuity equations about a uniform state gives the acoustic wave equation with c²=(∂p/∂ρ)_s. In a moving irrotational background the same perturbations propagate on Unruh's acoustic metric, the basis of analogue-gravity horizons. Viscosity and heat conduction add classical sound absorption.

name: Arnold: rigid body and ideal fluid as geodesics on groups
summary: Arnold (1966) showed that Euler's rigid-body equations are geodesic flow on SO(3) for the inertia metric, and that Euler's incompressible ideal-fluid equations are geodesic flow on the group of volume-preserving diffeomorphisms for the kinetic-energy metric. Both reduce to the same Euler–Arnold (Lie–Poisson) form, so energy–Casimir stability methods and curvature-based unpredictability estimates carry over between them.

name: Convection as the testbed for routes to chaos
summary: Convection sets in at Ra_c≈1708 through a pitchfork bifurcation of the conducting state. In small-aspect-ratio cells, Libchaber and Maurer observed period-doubling cascades with ratios approaching Feigenbaum's δ, and other cells showed quasiperiodic and intermittent routes. Together these confirmed bifurcation universality in a real fluid.
sources: Feigenbaum (1978). "Quantitative universality for a class of nonlinear transformations". *J. Stat. Phys.* 19, 25. [doi:10.1007/BF01020332](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01020332)

name: Lorenz equations: a truncated Rayleigh–Bénard model
summary: Lorenz's three ODEs are a three-mode Galerkin truncation (after Saltzman) of 2D Boussinesq convection: x is the roll amplitude, y and z are temperature modes, ρ=Ra/Ra_c and σ is the Prandtl number. The strange attractor of this truncation launched modern chaos theory.
breaks: Real convection near ρ≈28 is three-dimensional and far from three-mode; the equations are exact only for analogues such as the chaotic waterwheel and the single-mode laser.
sources: Rayleigh (1916). "On convection currents in a horizontal layer of fluid, when the higher temperature is on the under side". *Phil. Mag.* 32, 529. [doi:10.1080/14786441608635602](https://doi.org/10.1080/14786441608635602)

name: Convection rolls as the paradigm of pattern formation
summary: Rayleigh–Bénard convection above Ra_c≈1708 is the archetypal stationary pattern-forming instability (rolls, hexagons, Eckhaus and zigzag instabilities, spiral-defect chaos); near onset the roll envelope obeys the Ginzburg–Landau (Newell–Whitehead–Segel) amplitude equation, also derivable from the Swift–Hohenberg model.
sources: Rayleigh (1916). "On convection currents in a horizontal layer of fluid, when the higher temperature is on the under side". *Phil. Mag.* 32, 529. [doi:10.1080/14786441608635602](https://doi.org/10.1080/14786441608635602)
Cross & Hohenberg (1993). "Pattern formation outside of equilibrium". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 65, 851. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.65.851](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.65.851)

name: Faraday waves: Mathieu instability of a shaken fluid
summary: Shaking a liquid layer vertically modulates the effective gravity, so each surface-wave mode obeys a damped Mathieu equation (Benjamin–Ursell 1954). Above threshold the surface responds subharmonically, at half the drive frequency, and forms stripes, squares, hexagons and quasipatterns.
sources: Cross & Hohenberg (1993). "Pattern formation outside of equilibrium". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 65, 851. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.65.851](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.65.851)

name: Chaotic advection: the stream function as Hamiltonian
summary: Tracer motion in a 2D incompressible flow is a one-degree-of-freedom Hamiltonian system, with the stream function as H and (x,y) as the conjugate pair. Time-periodic stirring makes it non-autonomous, so even laminar Stokes flows mix chaotically (Aref's chaotic advection). The KAM islands that survive stay unmixed, which sets the design principle of microfluidic mixers.
breaks: Steady 3D flows are volume-preserving but not in general Hamiltonian; molecular diffusion eventually leaks across KAM-island barriers.
sources: Squires & Quake (2005). "Microfluidics: Fluid physics at the nanoliter scale". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 77, 977. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.77.977](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.77.977)

name: Falling cat and microswimmers: holonomy in shape space
summary: A cat reorients with zero angular momentum, and a Stokes swimmer advances with zero inertia; both do it by cycling their shape. The net rotation or displacement is the holonomy of a connection on shape space, set to leading order by the area the stroke encloses (Shapere–Wilczek). Purcell's scallop theorem says a reciprocal, zero-area stroke gives no net motion.
map: \Delta g=\oint\mathcal A(s)\,ds=\iint_S\mathcal F+\ldots;\quad\text{reciprocal stroke (zero area)}\Rightarrow\Delta g=0
breaks: The cat's connection comes from conserved (zero) angular momentum and its inertia tensor, an inertial constraint; the swimmer's comes from the viscous force-free and torque-free conditions, a dissipative one. The cat cannot shift its centre of mass, and the swimmer's displacement is independent of stroke rate only because inertia is absent.
sources: Purcell (1977). "Life at low Reynolds number". *Am. J. Phys.* 45, 3. [doi:10.1119/1.10903](https://doi.org/10.1119/1.10903)

name: Dynamical-systems routes to turbulence
summary: Bifurcation theory replaced Landau's picture of turbulence as an endless sequence of Hopf bifurcations. Ruelle and Takens predicted a strange attractor after only a few, which Gollub and Swinney confirmed in Taylor–Couette flow. Subcritical pipe-flow transition (Reynolds) is now framed through unstable exact coherent states, edge states and transient chaos.
sources: Reynolds (1883). "An experimental investigation of the circumstances which determine whether the motion of water shall be direct or sinuous, and of the law of resistance in parallel channels". *Phil. Trans. R. Soc.* 174, 935. [doi:10.1098/rstl.1883.0029](https://doi.org/10.1098/rstl.1883.0029)

name: Turbulence as high-dimensional deterministic chaos
summary: Turbulent flow is deterministic Navier–Stokes dynamics with positive Lyapunov exponents, so it is unpredictable beyond a few eddy times. The attractor dimension grows like the number of Kolmogorov-scale degrees of freedom, and the largest Lyapunov exponent scales with the inverse Kolmogorov time.
breaks: Low-dimensional attractor tools describe transition and small domains, not the developed multiscale cascade, which needs statistical (Kolmogorov) descriptions.
sources: Kolmogorov (1941; English translation 1991). "The local structure of turbulence in incompressible viscous fluid for very large Reynolds numbers". *Proc. R. Soc. A* 434, 9. [doi:10.1098/rspa.1991.0075](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1991.0075)

name: Lighthill's acoustic analogy: sound from turbulence
summary: Lighthill rearranged the exact flow equations into a wave equation driven by the turbulent Reynolds stress, which acts as a quadrupole source. It predicts that jet-noise power scales as U^8, with the radiated fraction of flow power ∝ Mach^5. This acoustic analogy founded aeroacoustics.

name: Bertrand's theorem and the Kepler–oscillator duality
summary: Bertrand's theorem: among central potentials, only 1/r and r² make every bounded orbit close. The two are dual. The conformal map z=w² with a time reparametrization (Bohlin, Levi-Civita; Kustaanheimo–Stiefel in 3D) sends centred oscillator ellipses to focal Kepler ellipses and exchanges the roles of energy and coupling constant.

name: Poincaré's three-body homoclinic tangle
summary: While correcting his 1889–90 prize memoir on the restricted three-body problem, Poincaré found that the stable and unstable manifolds of periodic orbits intersect transversally and fold into homoclinic tangles, the first recognition of deterministic chaos. Modern integrations show the inner Solar System is chaotic, with a Lyapunov time of ~5 Myr (Laskar).

name: Planetary stability: surviving tori and resonances
summary: KAM theory grew out of the perturbed Kepler problem. For small planetary masses most quasi-periodic orbits survive as invariant tori (Arnold's planetary theorem), while mean-motion and secular resonances carve out chaotic zones such as the Kirkwood gap at the 3:1 resonance with Jupiter. Hénon and Heiles showed that a third integral breaks down for galactic orbits.
sources: Hénon & Heiles (1964). "The applicability of the third integral of motion: Some numerical experiments". *Astron. J.* 69, 73. [doi:10.1086/109234](https://doi.org/10.1086/109234)

name: Gyroscopic stabilization: L4/L5 and the fast top
summary: The triangular Lagrange points L4/L5 are maxima of the rotating-frame effective potential, yet they are linearly stable below Routh's mass ratio because the Coriolis force is gyroscopic. The same mechanism holds a fast top upright. By the Kelvin–Tait–Chetaev theorem, dissipation destroys such gyroscopic stability; drag, for example, makes Trojan orbits drift away.

name: Euler's equations: Newton's law in the body frame
summary: Euler's equations are dL/dt=τ written in the co-rotating principal-axis frame using the transport theorem. The gyroscopic term ω×(Iω) is the rotational counterpart of the Coriolis and centrifugal terms that a particle feels in a rotating frame.

name: Driven nonlinear oscillators: bifurcations to chaos
summary: The Mathieu instability tongues are bifurcations of the oscillator's rest state. The driven Duffing oscillator shows saddle-node (jump) bifurcations and hysteresis in its response curve. The driven damped pendulum and Duffing oscillator reach chaos through period-doubling cascades with Feigenbaum's universal ratio δ≈4.669.
sources: Feigenbaum (1978). "Quantitative universality for a class of nonlinear transformations". *J. Stat. Phys.* 19, 25. [doi:10.1007/BF01020332](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01020332)

name: Tennis-racket instability and the sleeping-top threshold
summary: Linearizing Euler's equations about a principal axis gives centres for the largest and smallest moments and a saddle for the intermediate one, whose heteroclinic orbits are the Dzhanibekov flips. A sleeping heavy top loses stability when its spin falls below threshold, through a Hamiltonian–Hopf (Krein collision) bifurcation.

name: FPUT chain: normal modes, recurrence and solitons
summary: The Fermi–Pasta–Ulam–Tsingou anharmonic chain failed to share energy among its normal modes and showed near-recurrence. Zabusky and Kruskal took its continuum limit to the KdV equation and found solitons that pass through each other, which founded soliton theory. The chain lies close to the integrable Toda lattice.
sources: Zabusky & Kruskal (1965). "Interaction of 'Solitons' in a Collisionless Plasma and the Recurrence of Initial States". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 15, 240. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.15.240](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.15.240)

name: Limit-cycle oscillators, entrainment and Arnold tongues
summary: A self-sustained (van der Pol) oscillator has a neutrally stable phase, so weak periodic forcing or coupling can lock it. The phase difference obeys the Adler equation, and the locking regions in the drive-amplitude–detuning plane are Arnold tongues. Populations of such oscillators show the Kuramoto synchronization transition.
sources: Strogatz (2000). "From Kuramoto to Crawford: exploring the onset of synchronization in populations of coupled oscillators". *Physica D* 143, 1. [doi:10.1016/S0167-2789(00)00094-4](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0167-2789(00)00094-4)

name: Linear canonical transforms in Fresnel optics
summary: Paraxial propagation through any ABCD system is the Collins integral, which is the wave (metaplectic) representation of the linear canonical transformation given by the symplectic ray matrix. Free space acts as a Fresnel transform and a thin lens as a quadratic phase. A graded-index medium, whose ray Hamiltonian is a harmonic oscillator, performs a fractional Fourier transform that becomes the full Fourier transform after a quarter period.
breaks: The correspondence is exact only in the paraxial limit. Aberrations make the ray map nonlinear, and the wave propagator then stops being a simple metaplectic integral.

name: Eikonal equation is the Hamilton–Jacobi equation
summary: The wavefronts S=const of the eikonal equation |∇S|²=n² are level sets of Hamilton's characteristic function, and rays are its characteristics. Hamilton built this characteristic-function method for optics and carried it over to dynamics in 1834–35. Schrödinger later completed this optico-mechanical analogy into wave mechanics.

name: Ray optics as Hamiltonian flow; étendue as Liouville
summary: If the optical axis z is taken as time, rays obey Hamilton's equations with H=−√(n²−p²) and transverse momentum p=n sinθ. Paraxial ABCD matrices are symplectic in the reduced variables (y, nθ). Conservation of étendue and radiance is Liouville's theorem, and it caps solar concentration at n²/sin²θ_sun.
map: H=-\sqrt{n^2(\mathbf q,z)-\mathbf p^2};\ M^TJM=J\ (\det M=1\text{ in }(y,n\theta));\ n^2\,dA\,d\Omega=\text{const}
breaks: Liouville's theorem holds only for lossless systems without scattering. Diffraction blurs the phase-space picture at the scale of λ, where the Wigner function replaces the ray density.

name: Charged-particle Lagrangian and minimal coupling
summary: The Lorentz force follows from Lagrange's equations with the velocity-dependent potential U=q(φ−v·A), and the canonical momentum p=mv+qA differs from the kinetic momentum. A gauge transformation adds the total derivative q dχ/dt to L and leaves the motion unchanged. This is the classical root of gauge invariance and of the Aharonov–Bohm phase q∮A·dl/ħ.
map: L=\tfrac12mv^2-q\phi+q\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf A;\ \mathbf p=m\mathbf v+q\mathbf A;\ H=\frac{(\mathbf p-q\mathbf A)^2}{2m}+q\phi;\ L\to L+q\frac{d\chi}{dt}
breaks: Classically only the fields matter. That the potentials themselves have physical effects (the Aharonov–Bohm effect) appears only in quantum mechanics.

name: Fermat's principle and the principle of least action
summary: Light rays make the optical path stationary in the same way that mechanical trajectories make the action stationary. In Maupertuis' form δ∫p ds=0, ray optics maps onto mechanics with the refractive index in the role of momentum, so Snell's law becomes conservation of momentum parallel to the interface.
breaks: The map holds at fixed energy, which means a single frequency. The particle's speed is proportional to n, while light's phase velocity is c/n. Hamilton and de Broglie resolved this mismatch by distinguishing phase velocity from group velocity.
sources: Hamilton (1834). "On a General Method in Dynamics". *Phil. Trans. R. Soc.* 124, 247. [doi:10.1098/rstl.1834.0017](https://doi.org/10.1098/rstl.1834.0017)

name: Maxwell's equations from a field action
summary: Extending Hamilton's principle to fields, the inhomogeneous Maxwell equations come out as the Euler–Lagrange equations of the covariant action, and the homogeneous pair is the Bianchi identity of F=dA. Noether's theorem applied to this action gives the energy–momentum tensor. Gauge invariance of the coupling forces charge conservation.
breaks: The canonical Noether tensor is neither symmetric nor gauge invariant and needs the Belinfante improvement. The action also does not settle radiation reaction for point charges.

name: Photoelasticity: stress made visible by birefringence
summary: Stress makes a transparent solid birefringent in proportion to the difference of principal stresses (the stress-optic law, Brewster 1816). Viewed between crossed polarizers, a loaded model shows isochromatic fringes of σ1−σ2 and isoclinics along the principal directions, the classic tool of experimental stress analysis. The same photoelastic tensor drives acousto-optic modulators.
breaks: The method gives only stress differences and directions integrated through the thickness. Separating the individual principal stresses, or handling 3D bodies, needs extra methods such as stress freezing or scattered-light photoelasticity.

name: Elastic-solid aether and the Maxwell stress tensor
summary: Fresnel's transverse light waves led Cauchy, Green and MacCullagh to model light as waves in an elastic solid, and MacCullagh's rotationally elastic aether gave equations equivalent to Maxwell's in vacuum. Maxwell expressed electromagnetic forces as stresses in a medium. That is the origin of the stress tensor whose divergence gives the force density.
breaks: An ordinary elastic solid also carries longitudinal waves, which light lacks; this problem sank most elastic-aether theories. Relativity later removed the medium altogether.
sources: Maxwell (1865). "A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field". *Phil. Trans. R. Soc.* 155, 459. [doi:10.1098/rstl.1865.0008](https://doi.org/10.1098/rstl.1865.0008)

name: Vortex Biot–Savart law: vorticity as current
summary: An incompressible velocity field obeys ∇·u=0 and ∇×u=ω, the same equations as B with source μ0J. Vortex lines therefore induce velocity by the Biot–Savart law: a line vortex acts like a straight wire and a vortex ring like a current loop. Maxwell's 1861 molecular-vortex model ran the analogy the other way, to picture magnetic fields.
map: \mathbf u=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int\frac{\boldsymbol\omega'\times\mathbf R}{R^3}dV'\ \leftrightarrow\ \mathbf B=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int\frac{\mathbf J'\times\mathbf R}{R^3}dV',\ \mathbf R=\mathbf r-\mathbf r'
breaks: Vorticity is carried along and stretched by the velocity it induces (Helmholtz's laws), so vortex dynamics is nonlinear, whereas currents are prescribed. Parallel vortices of the same sign orbit each other instead of attracting the way parallel currents do.

name: Analogue event horizons in flows and optical fibres
summary: Sound in an irrotational flow travels on an effective acoustic metric, with a horizon where the flow outruns sound. In a fibre, the Kerr index front of a soliton moving at the group velocity acts as a horizon for probe light. Both therefore serve as analogue-gravity platforms for Hawking-type mode conversion.
map: ds^2\propto-(c_s^2-v^2)dt^2-2\mathbf v\cdot d\mathbf x\,dt+d\mathbf x^2;\quad \text{horizon at }|v|=c_s
breaks: Both rely on dispersion near the horizon. The fibre horizon is a moving index perturbation in a dispersive medium, not a flow, and claims of spontaneous Hawking-like emission in optics remain debated.

name: Hydrodynamics of light via the Madelung transform
summary: Writing the paraxial Kerr field as √ρ e^{iφ} turns the NLS into continuity and Euler equations for a compressible fluid. The nonlinearity supplies a pressure, and diffraction supplies a dispersive 'quantum pressure'. Defocusing media then show superfluid-like flow of light, optical vortices, and dispersive shock waves similar to undular bores.

name: Optical tweezers: Rayleigh-dipole force in a Stokes fluid
summary: A small dielectric bead is a Rayleigh scatterer. Its induced dipole is pulled up the intensity gradient while radiation pressure pushes it along the beam. In water it moves as an overdamped Brownian particle with Stokes drag, so the trap stiffness can be calibrated from the Lorentzian corner frequency. This makes tweezers a force probe for microfluidics and biophysics.
breaks: Beads comparable to λ need Mie or ray-optics force calculations. Near walls the Stokes drag increases (Faxén corrections).
sources: Ashkin (1970). "Acceleration and Trapping of Particles by Radiation Pressure". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 24, 156. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.24.156](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.24.156)

name: Atmospheric seeing: Kolmogorov turbulence limits coherence
summary: Kolmogorov scaling of temperature fluctuations makes the refractive-index structure function grow as r^(2/3), so starlight picks up a phase structure function proportional to (r/r0)^(5/3). The Fried parameter r0 sets the spatial coherence length and limits telescope resolution to about λ/r0. The result is speckle, which motivated speckle interferometry and adaptive optics.
breaks: Real atmospheric turbulence has finite outer and inner scales and is intermittent, so the 5/3 law fails at the largest and smallest separations.
sources: Kolmogorov (1941; English translation 1991). "The local structure of turbulence in incompressible viscous fluid for very large Reynolds numbers". *Proc. R. Soc. A* 434, 9. [doi:10.1098/rspa.1991.0075](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1991.0075)

name: Inverse-square law: Kepler orbits and Coulomb fields
summary: Newtonian gravity and electrostatics share Poisson's equation and the 1/r Green's function. Gauss's law, the shell theorem and the conserved Runge–Lenz vector therefore carry over between them. Rutherford scattering is the hyperbolic Kepler orbit in a repulsive Coulomb field.
breaks: Gravity has only one sign of charge, so it has no screening, no dipole radiation and no gravitational conductor. Gravitational charge also equals inertial mass, which has no electric counterpart.

name: Larmor radiation and the collapse of classical atoms
summary: An electron on a classical Kepler orbit around a nucleus radiates at the Larmor rate and spirals inward within about 10⁻¹¹ s. This failure of Rutherford's planetary atom motivated Bohr's stationary orbits. The same radiative decay of orbits shapes cyclotron and synchrotron motion.
breaks: In quantum mechanics there is no continuous inspiral. Stationary states replace it, and radiation occurs only in transitions at discrete frequencies.

name: Field momentum restores momentum conservation
summary: Magnetic forces between moving charges violate Newton's third law, so mechanical momentum alone is not conserved. Maxwell's theory restores conservation of linear and angular momentum by giving the field a momentum density ε0E×B and a stress tensor. Feynman's disk paradox and hidden momentum are standard examples.
breaks: Inside matter, how momentum splits between the field and the medium is ambiguous; this is the Abraham–Minkowski controversy.

name: Galilean kinematics vs Lorentz-covariant electrodynamics
summary: Maxwell's equations are not invariant under Galilean boosts, as the magnet-and-conductor asymmetry and the fixed speed of light show. Resolving this clash with Newtonian kinematics produced the Lorentz transformations and Einstein's 1905 relativity. Under relativity, Newton's second law becomes the covariant Lorentz-force equation.

name: Foucault pendulum and Rytov rotation: one holonomy
summary: Each day, the Foucault pendulum's swing plane turns by the solid angle 2π(1−cosϑ) enclosed by the local vertical, where ϑ is the colatitude; this is parallel transport on a sphere. The polarization of light in a helically coiled fibre rotates by the solid angle swept by its propagation direction (the Rytov–Vladimirskii rotation, observed by Tomita and Chiao). Both are the same geometric phase.
breaks: The pendulum carries a classical vector across Earth's surface. For photons the rotation is a helicity-dependent Berry phase ±σΩ, with opposite signs for the two circular polarizations.

name: Larmor's theorem: Coriolis force mimics a magnetic field
summary: In a frame rotating at Ω, the Coriolis force 2m v×Ω has the same form as the magnetic force q v×B. Rotating at Ω=−qB/2m therefore removes a weak uniform field to first order, which explains the Larmor precession of orbits and atomic diamagnetism. Conversely, rotating neutral systems can simulate magnetic fields.
breaks: The equivalence holds only to first order. The rotating frame adds a centrifugal force of order Ω² with no magnetic counterpart, which must be small or cancelled by a trap.
